comments.text: Configure the game's vectors and raster chain, select VIC bank $C000, clear the screen and colour RAM, initialise sprite registers and the music, then wait in the title-state main loop.
Requested level number, 0 through 4, read by the selector and level loader.
Last level number accepted by the loader; compared with the requested number to avoid a disk load when its payload is already resident.
Unused byte between the loaded-level number and the title delay, holding 0: no instruction reads or writes it.
Title delay and main-loop gate. The title IRQ advances it to 50 before accepting fire; play initialisation clears it.
A value of 1 requests the per-level Monty initialisation routine at $1786, which clears it after setting his state.
High-score name cheat selector. Terrain, weapon and pickup paths test this byte for the selected exception.
Nonzero selects the sound-effects path in the play IRQ; zero selects the music path. Direction input on the title toggles it.

Temporary selector controlling whether line-motion initialisation ($3FB7) removes the offsets it adds to its target, 6 in X and 5 in Y. Both are in the routine's half-resolution coordinates, so 12 and 10 pixels. The routine clears the flag after using it.
Temporary horizontal displacement used by direction-mask movement and supporting actors.
Temporary vertical displacement used by direction-mask movement.
Selects the $E800 or $EC00 screen buffer for drawing, terrain probes and the VIC screen pointer.
Unused byte before the actor bit-mask table, holding 0: no instruction reads or writes it.
Eight powers of two, one for each sprite slot or completed-level bit.
Cumulative low-bit masks used by the level selector to skip completed destinations.
Direction remapping table used to reverse path-facing masks and timed actor turns.
A nonzero value suppresses the camera-follow scroll request in $593C.
Auxiliary state cleared at the end of the quit transition.
Quit/high-score transition counter. Its initial value clears actors and the screen, later milestones draw the final score and return to the title.

Pause and temporary gameplay-inhibition flag, tested by the three play raster handlers and by the RUN/STOP check. P toggles it; the level-selector preparation at $1778 stores 2, Monty's level initialisation at $17A5 clears it, and super weapons, level completion and spawn seeking also write it.
Extra energy refill available at zero energy. The damage routine consumes it before beginning death.
Countdown for the charged enemy's colour and facing-dependent damage effect.
Slot of the actor whose charge animation and palette effect $4E8E follows.
Set by fire in the selector; the main loop responds by calling the level loader.
Byte offset of the accepted high-score name, later used by the secret-name checker.
Per-level initial shape, X-low, Y, X-high, Y-high and related initialisation values. The level initialiser indexes these arrays by current level.
Five little-endian scroll-limit words, indexed by level. The camera follower compares the world column against the selected limit.
Base capacity copied into $091F at a new game, with exceptions selected by secret high-score names.
Initial strength copied into $7F79 when Monty is initialised for a level.
Initial reserve copied into $08E3 on a new game.
Maximum count of full segments in the energy bar. The energy limit is twice this value.
Incremented by the final play raster band, and by the selector's top band while the level selector runs. Used to pace the main loop and alternating gameplay work.
Counter incremented and decremented around the play raster bands' work.
Unused byte next to the raster counters, holding 1: no instruction reads or writes it.
Set after the colour update and tested by the middle raster band's gameplay gate.
Unused byte before the vector installer, holding 2: no instruction reads or writes it.
Disable interrupts, install the RAM IRQ dispatcher at $0E79, reset trap at $0E6A and NMI return at $0E69, enable the display and bank RAM with I/O visible using processor port $35.

Disable CIA1 interrupts, clear the raster high bit and schedule the title handler at $0B45 through the indirect IRQ pointer $B8/$B9. Enable raster interrupts at line 1 and return with interrupts enabled.

Acknowledge the raster IRQ and schedule the next band at line 176. Apply horizontal fine scroll, select the level's character set and colours, publish sprite pointers, scan controls and update gameplay when its pause and transition gates permit. Select music or effects with $08BF.

Schedule the next raster band at line 255. Update the screen colours and, when scrolling, pause and transition gates permit, run collision, enemy and weapon work before returning through the shared IRQ epilogue.

Schedule the next frame's top band at line 57. Clear horizontal fine scroll, select the status character set, update end-of-frame graphics and sprite registers, increment the frame counter and select the active screen buffer.

Schedule the second title band at line 150, select the title character set and update its music and display. Advance the initial delay $08BC up to 50, then test joystick fire to start a new game, clear score digits and initialise its state.
Schedule the title's top handler at line 10, select the title colours and fill the screen's side columns and their colour cells before returning through the shared IRQ epilogue.

Schedule the level-selection scene's second raster band at line 150. Draw actors, compare Monty's coordinates with the level's selector position, choose adjacent unfinished levels with joystick left/right, and latch fire into $08E6 to request a load. The completed-level mask $260E gates the fifth level.
Schedule the selector's top handler at line 10 and restore its background and shared character colours for the lower screen.
Restore Y, X and A from the stack in reverse order and return from the raster interrupt.
Return immediately from an NMI.
Disable interrupts, reset the stack and decimal mode, switch the display off and loop incrementing the border colour.
Save A, X and Y and jump through $00B8/$00B9, whose target each raster handler changes to its successor.
Decrement $7F9C when nonzero. On even frame-counter values, run $1AE0, $1415 and $1A53; odd values return immediately.

Drive the eight keyboard columns through CIA1 port A, find a pressed row and translate its column/row position through the key table into $8A71. With no key pressed clear that byte, then return CIA1 port A to inputs.
A indexes the keyboard-column and row-mask tables at $8A72 and $8AFD. Drive that column and return A=1 if its row is pressed, otherwise A=0 and restore CIA1 port A to inputs.

Copy eight actor positions and colours into the VIC sprite registers using the register-offset table at $8B96. Apply hit flashes, hide coordinates outside the supported high-byte range, and rebuild X-high, expansion and multicolour masks. Clear both screens' sprite pointers before their later publication.

Interpret the translated key byte: P toggles pause unless a super weapon is running ($89CD nonzero); SPACE starts the super weapon when none is running, no guardian is active ($835E zero) and a charge is left at $89CC; RUN/STOP sets the quit transition while paused. Recognised commands clear the key latch.
Restore the title raster chain, start its delay and initialise the music with $66FF cleared.

Set Monty's collision dimensions, count the animation delay and select a new sequence when facing or movement state changes. Read sprite numbers from $7EF9 and interpret $80 as a loop followed by a sequence index.

Choose an index in the animation stream from facing, movement state and the hazard countdown $7EF6, which selects other sequences for standing and walking. The jumping state uses a random bit. A facing change while walking can discard this call's return address to finish in the caller's caller.
Unless $7EF6 is set, compare facing with the saved value. On a change, save it, select sprite $14 and a three-step animation delay, then discard one return address before returning.
For levels other than 2 and 3, count down $8B89 and rotate four glyph-row bytes at $F398, $F39F, $F3A7 and $F3A0 every second call, reinserting each bit that shifts out.

Count down $8B88 and dispatch level-specific character-memory changes: rotating rows and circulating bytes at fixed addresses in the level's $F000 character set. Each level sets its own next delay; level 0 also moves the $F008 strip at the halfway count.
Rotate the 32-byte strip at $F008 one byte towards higher addresses, wrapping its last byte to its first.
Rotate four character rows at $F708, $F70C, $F701 and $F705 twice per update and reload the character-animation delay with 6.
Rotate $F280 left with wrap and reload the character-animation delay with 2.

Rotate nine selected rows between $F688 and $F7D4 left with wrap, then move $F7E0-$F7EE up one byte and store the old $F7EF at $F7E1: this circulates the 15 bytes $F7E1-$F7EF and leaves $F7E0 unchanged. Reload the character-animation delay with 4.
Rotate the selected character rows at $F550-$F7EC, replace $F7D8 with a random byte and rotate $F7E2 twice. Reload the character-animation delay with 5.
When $7F7C is at least 2 and the current Monty sprite number is below $17, add $16 to select its corresponding alternate shape.
On transition 1 clear the screen and eight actor slots, then advance the transition counter. At 5 call $1B65; at 100 clear the transition's state bytes and return to the title handler.
Scan active actor slots 2 through 7. Remove an actor with a nonzero Y high byte, X high byte $FF and low X below $F8, or X high byte 1 and low X at least $68, by calling $4460 with its slot in Y.

Manage the shop state $8090. At 1, initialise the companion sprite in slot 1. From 3 up, pay for a bought item: once a call, take one coin from $7F78 unless the joystick's left or right push differs from the last one, kept in $809C, then count $8090 down, so the payment lasts as many calls as the price. Below 3, show the response message, or leave the shop on fire when Monty touches the exit sprite. A separate timer removes actor type 9 when it expires.
Set up sprite slot 1 beside Monty with shape $61, colour 0 and 21-by-21 dimensions, clear its expansion flags and advance the item-message state.

Use actor Y's type to select a 16-byte message at $80DC. Draw it in the top row with colour 9, mapping spaces to blank glyph 7. For types below 8 temporarily display the amount at $809A using the money-number routine.
Count down $80D9. When it reaches zero, scan active slots 2 through 7 and remove those whose type is 9.
Toggles between the title picture and high-score display after the title's 250-call counter.
Counter advanced by $153A; at 250 it changes the title view and resets to zero.

Update the high-score entry state, alternate the title picture and score table after a 250-call counter, draw the music/effects selection glyph and toggle that option when joystick direction bits are active.

Copy six 36-character lines of the ending text into the screen. Count the initial acknowledgement delay; fire after it sets the quit state, clears selector state and returns the raster chain to the title.

Compare the requested and loaded level numbers and call the disk loader at $0400 when they differ. If the payload's identifier at $7EC0 then differs from the requested level, jump back to $1602, which calls the loader again: the loaded level $08BA is set only after a match ($16E7). Then install the play raster handlers, clear the transition flags and publish the loaded level.
Original five filename pointers retained beside the loader, superseded by the Dynamix disk loader.
Original two-byte level filename strings retained in the engine image.
Main-loop request to rebuild the level screens and initialise their spawn cursor.

Prepare the new main-loop state, reset scroll coordinates and set the spawn-column progress byte $8C49 to 99. Wait for the raster frame counter before scrolling and running gameplay main-loop work; dispatch title and level-load transitions through $260F and $08E6.
Wait for the raster frame counter $0920 to change, then dispatch scrolling, new-player setup and main-loop updates while $08BC permits gameplay.
Watch $260F for the level-selector transition, run its preparation once, and call the level loader when $08E6 is set. Return to new-game main-loop initialisation when $260F becomes zero.

When $08BD equals 1, clear transient weapon, death and pause state, set the movement and energy-related counters, clear eight actor slots and initialise Monty's coordinates, shape and colour from the current level's tables (his collision dimensions are set by $101C). Copy the level's background colour, attack delays and scroll limit. Unless effects are selected, stop the music and request tune 0, the tune the title also requests.
Clear 25 rows of the screen at $EC00 with an inclusive X loop from 40 down to 0. The extra column overlaps the next row.
Fill the playfield colour rows from $D828 through $DB98 with A, using an inclusive X loop from 40 down to 0.
Six mutable decimal character digits, least significant first, followed by six display-order digits saved by the score renderer.
Add Y units at decimal digit X in $191F, repeatedly incrementing the digit and propagating overflow above character 9 to the next digit. Digits are character codes beginning at $30.
Add one unit at score digit 0 through the decimal character-digit accumulator.
Add one unit at score digit 2 through the decimal character-digit accumulator.
Add two units at score digit 2 through the decimal character-digit accumulator.
Add four units at score digit 2 through the decimal character-digit accumulator.
Add eight units at score digit 2 through the decimal character-digit accumulator.
Add six units at digit 2 and one at digit 3, using the accumulator's carry between decimal character digits.
Add two units at digit 2 and three at digit 3 using the score accumulator.
Add two units at score digit 4 through the decimal character-digit accumulator.
Combine CIA1 timer A and B bytes with additions and a final XOR to return a changing random byte in A.
Fill 41 status colour cells from $8BE4 and blank the first row of both screen buffers with glyph 7.
Restore status colours and blank columns 21 through 39 of the first row in the $E800 screen buffer.

When $08BC is zero, reverse the six score digits into their saved display order and the status screen. Suppress leading zeroes, retaining the units digit, and copy status columns 1 through 39 to the second screen.
Clear the bar area, draw one full segment per pair of energy units at $7F77 and a half segment for an odd final unit. Fill the remainder up to the capacity $091F with empty-segment glyphs.
Increment the energy-bar capacity and clamp values of 17 or above to 17.
Decrement the energy-bar capacity, replacing an exact zero result with 1.
Number of one-unit restoration steps still to perform through $1A53.
While $1A52 is nonzero, decrement it and add one to $7F77. Clamp energy to twice the capacity at $091F.

Return during a hit flash or an existing death state. Otherwise decrement energy. At zero consume a reserve at $08E3 and refill to $091F, or begin death if no reserve remains. A surviving hit starts a 14-call flash counter.
Advance a death subcounter to 20 before changing the death stage. The first two stages select sprites $5A and $5B; stage 6 requests the quit/high-score transition.
Draw strength $7F79 as full icons from $E80A, filling the remainder of three positions with empty icons when strength is 1 or 2. With strength 0 the routine returns without drawing anything.
Decrement the weapon-strength index, replacing an underflow result of $FF with zero.
Increment the weapon-strength index, replacing an exact result of 4 with 3.
Draw the unsigned amount $7F78 as three decimal characters by repeated subtraction of 100 and 10. Suppress leading zeroes with glyph 7. The alternate entry $1B23 uses X as a screen-column offset.
Write the amount at $7F78 in three decimal character cells beginning at $E80F+X. X is the initial column offset; the routine changes X while suppressing leading zeroes.
Draw the final-scene label, saved six score digits and the current level's 23-character title using the offset table $8498.

When no supporting actor is latched, compare Monty's high coordinate bytes and feet height against actor X, then compare their absolute horizontal distance with an asymmetric bound derived from the actor width. Store X in $7EF2 on success, otherwise clear it.

With a supporting actor latched, resolve Monty's movement state and, while the support flag at $38B4 permits, apply the actor's displacement through $241E. Place Monty 21 pixels above the supporting actor. One actor state uses $8C44 for both displacement bytes.
Two low X coordinate choices for the mine guardian's random initial position.
Two Y coordinate choices for the mine guardian's random initial position.
Guardian health accumulator, initialised to 60 and reduced by weapon damage; a borrow starts level completion.

When the guardian state $835E is nonzero, dispatch by the current level. Each guardian builds linked components from actor templates and updates its own phase, movement bounds, animations and attack timing.

Build the mine guardian from slots 4 through 7, place its leading component at one of two random X and Y choices, link the remaining components, set two guardian counters and advance its initialisation state.

Handle the Orient guardian's initialisation and subsequent movement. Build four components from templates $5F, $60, $61 and $62; change its direction on map probes and coordinate limits, and occasionally start an attack.

Probe terrain for guardian slots 4 through 7 through $3E9F, then test slot 4's coordinates and the horizontal and vertical terrain probes. Reverse the relevant direction bits at a boundary and update the components' shape/animation settings. A rare random value starts the three secondary components' attack state.

Toggle horizontal direction bits $0C for slots 5 through 7, then load the shapes of slots 4 through 7 from the direction-dependent tables at $8C0C-$8C13, and set the animation indexes $873C/$873D and flag bytes $872C/$872D of slots 4 and 5 from immediate values chosen by the new direction.
Toggle vertical direction bits $03 for guardian slots 5 through 7.
For level 2 initialise or update the linked two-part guardian. Spawn its attacks when the component animation reaches specific shapes, and advance the guardian phase after a 65-call counter.
Build linked slots 6 and 7 from templates $87 and $88. Randomly choose the first component's X coordinate from $8C15 and place it at Y=$98; link the second 21 pixels below.

For level 3 create templates $B9 and $BA in slots 6 and 7, link their positions and initialise guardian counters; later probe slot 6's terrain through $3E9F and reverse horizontal direction on its coordinate or terrain-probe boundary.
Toggle horizontal direction bits $0C in the two component slots 6 and 7.

Initialise the final guardian with templates $ED-$EF in slots 6, 7 and 5, then keep its components aligned and step its command sequence every 32 calls, except while its action state $87A7 is 2, when the countdown at $8C1F stands still. The index $8C14 starts at zero and is incremented before each read, so the commands come from $8C21 on and the byte at $8C20 is never run; $FF sets the index back to zero. Its commands change attack and motion state.

Align the guardian's secondary shapes with slot 7, inspect its action state and execute the timed commands from $8C20. Set the affected component animation and motion bytes, then randomise the colours of type-zero slots 2 through 4.
While the level-1 guardian is active, place slot 4 horizontally 24 pixels left of slot 5 and vertically 21 pixels above slot 6.

Subtract weapon damage $477F from the guardian's health at $1CA5. A borrow triggers component destruction, clears its active state, starts the completion counter and adds 20000 points. Otherwise flash its components; the Iceland guardian also changes shape by remaining health and can spawn template $BB.

Probe terrain around actor X, then build its direction mask from relative X/Y position when the corresponding steering flags permit and the terrain probes are below 3. Update the saved horizontal facing and reset its animation when that facing changes.

Count down the temporary state $7EF6: above $62 keep actions inhibited, at $62 release them, and at 1 force a new animation choice. With no countdown, or with one below $62, terrain class 10 at either top-row centre probe ($8600/$8601) starts a timed sprite-$5D damage response when Monty is standing or walking, and otherwise puts him in the falling state.
Set the temporary hazard countdown to $80, select Monty sprite $5D, inhibit selected actions, reset the animation delay and call the damage routine.
Decode direction bits 2 and 3 from A and move Monty left or right through the collision-aware movement routines, using $08C1 as the displacement.

Set the title's multicolour values and copy six 21-character rows from $8576-$85F3 into the screen. Add the fire prompt and copyright lines, with changing prompt colours derived from the CIA random routine.

While $835F is nonzero, count it up by one each call. While it is below 125, convert one unit of remaining energy and of money, and the super-weapon state, into points on each call. At 125 prepare the departure animation; at 250 set the selector transition and OR this level's bit into $260E.

Install the level-selection raster chain, clear the screen, initialise Monty's selector position and five marker sprites, and select the marker shape for each completed level from the mask at $260E. Draw the selector's fixed labels unless all five bits are set.
Bits 0 through 4 record completed levels; the selector requires the first four bits to reach the final level.
Main-loop transition state: zero runs play initialisation, one requests selector preparation and two means the selector is active.
Five low X positions for the level-marker sprites.
Five high X bytes for the level-marker sprites.
Common Y coordinate for the level-marker sprites.

Copy the level selector's five framed level pictures, 22 rows of six characters at $8634-$86B7, to the screen, then colour the four middle columns of each picture's four rows: 9 for the first and fourth pictures, 13 for the third and fifth. The second picture and the frames keep the colour the screen was filled with.
Select a 23-character level title using the requested level number $08B9 and the offset table $8498, and copy it to $EE8A with colour 9.
Unsigned pixel displacement read by the four actor coordinate helpers.
Subtract the displacement $2718 from actor X's 16-bit Y coordinate at $86C8/$86D8, propagating borrow into the high byte.
Add the displacement $2718 to actor X's 16-bit Y coordinate at $86C8/$86D8, propagating carry into the high byte.
Subtract the displacement $2718 from actor X's 16-bit X coordinate at $86C0/$86D0, propagating borrow into the high byte.
Add the displacement $2718 to actor X's 16-bit X coordinate at $86C0/$86D0, propagating carry into the high byte.

Compare actors X and Y using signed horizontal and vertical differences and their collision dimensions at $86F0/$86F8. Select the bound from the actor on the relevant side. Return carry set for overlap and clear for separation; the code patches its immediate bounds and uses $27DD/$27DE as scratch.
Scratch horizontal origin used when converting a sprite coordinate to a screen-cell column.
Scratch vertical origin used by the attack's terrain probe.
Low byte of the temporary absolute coordinate difference in the actor box test.
High byte of the temporary coordinate difference in the actor box test.
Eight unused zero bytes between the overlap scratch and the terrain-probe routine: no instruction reads or writes them.

Convert Monty's screen coordinates to character-cell coordinates, accounting for fine scroll. Patch two screen reads from the active buffer's row-pointer table; both read the same cell, in his feet row. Translate its character code through the level's class table at $AF00 into both $18 and $24.

Build row pointers for the active screen buffer and sample the character cells around Monty's left, right, head and feet. Translate their character codes through $AF00. Clear selected probes according to movement state and vertical alignment, and set $2BDC when aligned on the eight-pixel standing grid.

Translate the sampled character codes into terrain classes using the level's $AF00 table. Clear the two extra side probes $8602/$8603 outside climbing state, then retain the relevant top or bottom side probes according to Monty's Y alignment, which it records in $2BDC.
Set when Monty's Y lies on the eight-pixel grid used for standing and leaving ladders.

When Monty has no supporting actor and is neither jumping nor blocked in a climbing pose, inspect his feet classes. Move him down, probe again and switch to falling state; landing restores standing state and snaps his Y coordinate to the eight-pixel grid based at 53.
Shifted copy of the active-low joystick bits while the movement handlers consume them.
Saved five-bit joystick state, also read by animation and sliding-terrain handling.
Dispatch movement state $7F43: 0 and 1 use the standing/walking input handler, 2 uses the jump trajectory, 3 uses falling input and 4 uses climbing controls.

Enforce the right coordinate bound and reject terrain classes at or above 4, or 3 while climbing, at the right-side probes. Terrain class 8 alternates motion by frame parity and selects a sound. On an accepted step add $2718 to Monty's X coordinate.

Enforce the left coordinate bound and reject terrain classes at or above 4, or 3 while climbing, at the left-side probes. Terrain class 8 alternates motion by frame parity and selects a sound. On an accepted step subtract $2718 from Monty's X coordinate.
Reject an upward move if either head probe has terrain class 4 or above; otherwise move Monty up by $2718.

Move Monty down when both feet probes have classes below 2, then probe again. On landing from jumping state, restore standing, reset the trajectory index to 3 and snap Y to the eight-pixel grid based at 53.
Move Monty down by $2718 when the lower centre probe has terrain class below 3.

Read the five active-low joystick bits. Neutral input sets standing state; otherwise set walking, decode up for jumping or climbing, down for entering a ladder, left/right for collision-aware motion and fire for the attack routine.
If the upper centre probe is class 1, attempt an upward move and enter climbing state. Otherwise enter jumping state, save horizontal intent from the joystick and select the jump sound.
Read the stick while falling. Up enters climbing on class-1 terrain; left and right change facing and apply collision-aware horizontal motion.

Allow up to enter a climb on class 1 or 2, and fire to attack. Apply the saved horizontal intent, then read a signed displacement from $7F45 indexed by $7F72. Negative values move up, nonnegative values move down, and $80 ends the trajectory and restores standing state.
Check whether Monty remains supported by a ladder, then decode up, down, left and right to the appropriate collision-aware movement routines with a one-pixel step.
When $2BDC marks alignment and the lower centre class is at least 2, restore standing state and discard the current call's return address to leave the climb handler early.

Dispatch feet terrain classes 5 and 6 to timed conveyor motion, class 7 to sliding in Monty's facing direction, and class 9 to a jump/damage response after a two-call counter. The state in $08BE can suppress that damage.

When Monty's Y is below 38 or at least 246, compute his world block from scroll position and X. Search the level's exit tables for a matching edge and block, then replace the scroll pointers, position Monty on the opposite edge and set the jump or falling state.
Index the current level's 12-byte shop record at $809D, load its first scroll/position tuple and request a screen rebuild.
X selects a six-byte destination record: two scroll words followed by block X and Y coordinates. Convert the block coordinates to Monty's pixels, request a screen rebuild and restore standing state.
While fire is pressed, clear the shop state, start a 32-call shop-entry delay and load the second six-byte destination tuple for this level.

Suppress fire during the temporary hazard state. In a shop, compare money with the selected item's price and dispatch an affordable purchase; otherwise check attack cooldown, movement state and slot-1 availability, then select the attack pose and projectile setup from weapon and strength.
While the recoil counter $7F82 is nonzero, decrement it and move Monty one pixel in the direction saved at $7F83, away from the way he faces, through the terrain-aware movement routines.

Activate slot 1 and select its sprite, colour, collision dimensions and probe offsets from the weapon and strength tables. Place it relative to Monty and configure type-specific animation, homing and expansion flags. The damage is looked up later, by the hit test at $46FD.

Outside shop state, expire a basic attack, move the type-1 projectile along its signed trajectory, move or home type 2 according to strength, and move type 3 horizontally while cycling its colour. Restore the basic weapon after its lifetime expires, unless the name modifier $08BE is 2.

Temporarily shift Monty's X four pixels right and test his box against visible active slots 2 through 7. Dispatch contacts, restore his X and clear the selected shop price when the shop state is active.

In a shop, derive the contacted actor's price and display its message, unwinding the contact caller. Outside a shop, dispatch actor type to pickup, shop entry, score, damage or special-effect handling.

Dispatch actor Y's type: 1/2/3 select timed weapons; 4 adds strength; 5 restores energy; 6 and $37 add 25 money; 7 grows energy capacity; 8 gives a reserve; 9 enters a shop on down; $0A-$0D add score. Other types select special collision responses or ordinary damage.

Continue the contact-type dispatch for strength, food, money, capacity, shopkeeper, points and reserve items. Pickups remove their actor through $4460 and, except the capacity item, select the pickup sound; the shopkeeper instead enters a separate screen.
Ignore the invulnerable marker $FE and actor type $0E; convert selected types into a timed effect, handle the heavy-damage and hazard types, or call Monty's ordinary damage routine.
Clear the contacted actor's active flag, X low/high, Y low, sprite, type and motion state (Y high is retained), select the damage sound and apply damage to Monty.
Call the damage entry $1A71 seven times before removing this contact actor and applying the final ordinary hit.
Call the damage entry $1A71 twice, then use the hazard-removal path which applies another ordinary hit.
Start the temporary terrain-hazard response through $2403, select Monty sprite $14 and remove the contact actor through the ordinary hazard path.

Scan slots 1 through 7. Count active and animation delays, read shape bytes from $8EC0 plus each actor's animation index, treat $FF followed by an index as a loop and $FF/$FF as removal, and store the next sprite number.
Use actor X's type and horizontal direction to select an animation-stream index from the left/right tables at $87D0 and $88BF, and clear its animation delay.

Flag for ride_supporting_actor ($1C27). update_other_actors ($38B5) clears it on entry and increments it at $38F7 when the slot whose motion work it is about to run on this call is the actor supporting Monty ($7EF2). $1C62 reads it and leaves Monty unmoved while it is zero, so he is carried only on the calls in which his supporting actor takes its turn.

Scan active slots 2 through 7. Probe support candidates, alternate motion work between slot groups on frame parity, dispatch flag-controlled special handling and motion states 1 through 5, then apply the supporting actor's displacement to Monty.

One byte, 1, between update_other_actors and the type-$0E terrain-actor updater at $3962. No instruction in the resident part or in any level names, indexes or points at it: nothing reads or writes it.
Scan slots 2 through 7 and run the screen-trail drawing routine $3D82 for active actor type $0E.
Decode A's low four bits as up, down, left and right, applying each set direction through the coordinate helpers with actor X and displacement $2718.
Absolute horizontal distance scratch for the homing-direction calculation.
Low-byte absolute vertical difference scratch for homing.
Saved low-byte horizontal distance used by the six-pixel near-axis test.
Low-four-bit direction mask from actor X towards actor Y.
Compute the low-byte absolute Y difference and 16-bit absolute X difference from actor X to actor Y. Build a direction mask in $399F and remove an axis when its saved low-byte difference is below 6.
Compare the desired direction at $399F with the saved attack direction. Use circular eight-direction lookup tables to turn one step towards it, gated by a three-call turn delay.

Temporarily inhibit gameplay and scan four-byte spawn records from $A000 until the record's two-byte position is at or beyond the scroll position. Save the byte offset at $8C47/$8C48 and release the inhibition flag.
Add four to the spawn-record byte offset at $8C47/$8C48 with carry.
After a screen rebuild, initialise the spawn-record cursor and scan the visible 40-column span. For records matching each world column, call the actor-spawn routine and advance the record cursor.
Search slots 2 through 7 for an active byte equal to zero. Return X as that slot, or 8 when all six are occupied.

Find a free actor slot and read the current four-byte record through $98/$99. Five special identifiers activate a guardian; $FB returns without spawning. Other identifiers choose a 26-byte template through the low/high halves of its pointer directory, then position the actor from the record's row and visible column.
Read the template pointer from $817C+Y into $A8/$A9 and populate actor X through the shared template reader at $3C32.

Read 26 successive bytes through $A8/$A9 into actor X's shape, colour, dimensions, health, flags, type, animation and motion arrays. Copy the animation delay into its reload value, clear horizontal expansion and mark the actor active.
At spawn-column marker 40, test the next spawn record against the world column at the screen's entering edge. Spawn and advance when its position matches.

When the screen's initial population is complete and a random low-three-bit test succeeds, select a four-byte record using the level's mask and pointer tables. Spawn it if its position lies within the visible 40 columns.

Save an actor's initial Y and derive its screen row. For visible columns, draw paired character and colour bytes down the active screen buffer between its original and current heights, then extend the tail while the sampled terrain class is 0 or 10. A flag can turn an encountered obstruction into a path reversal.

Sample six character cells around actor X from the active screen buffer, compensating for dimensions and fine scroll. Clamp the sample column into the visible interval and translate the characters through $AF00 into the actor's six terrain-probe arrays.
Two bytes before line-motion setup. Nothing reads or writes $3FB1. $3FB2 temporarily holds a coordinate high byte while initialise_line_motion ($3FB7) halves the 9-bit coordinate.
Use Monty as target Y=0 and a motion speed of 1, then initialise the straight-line movement state through $3FB7.

A gives movement speed and Y selects the target actor. Work in half-resolution coordinates, compute signed X/Y differences and their absolute magnitudes, choose unit direction steps and an error accumulator, then restore full coordinates. $08C0 can remove the target offsets before the calculation.

Optionally remove an actor on solid terrain, then advance its line-motion error accumulator for the configured speed. Stop its motion state when both target coordinates match. Preserve coordinate low bits while converting to and from half-resolution arithmetic.

Select magnitude and direction streams through the path pointer directories at $90E0 and $9104. Apply the current displacement, update animation on facing changes, and advance the path index forwards or backwards. Values $FC-$FF reverse, stop, loop or hold the path according to the tested command.

Six shape substitutions for the path-driven actor types $2B-$2F. On every ordinary path step whose direction byte $8778,X is nonzero, $423D replaces the actor's shape $90-$95 with the entry here ($92 for $90-$92, $95 for $93-$95) and stores 3 in $8740,X.
Negate the actor's signed path-index step and apply that new step to its path index.
Select special terrain steering from actor mode $8798, optionally remove the actor on a random flag test, then move it using its direction mask and X/Y displacement bytes.
Decode A's direction bits. Move actor X up/down using $08C2 and left/right using $08C1 through the 16-bit coordinate helpers.
If actor X's first terrain probe is class 4 or above, clear its active byte, sprite and Y low byte (Y high is retained).
Probe actor X's terrain. Reverse horizontal direction when its support probes fall below 2, side probes reach 4 or its screen-edge coordinate test requires it.

For mode $FF, stop path motion on supporting terrain and select a type-dependent animation and sound. For mode $FE, stop a downward path when the vertical terrain tests accept a landing; actor type $6E selects a fixed landed shape.
Probe actor X's terrain. Set the falling flag when both support probes are below 2, and reverse horizontal motion against side classes 4 or above.
Probe terrain and move actor X down two pixels while both support classes are below 2. Otherwise clear its falling flag.
Count the actor's turn timer up to its limit, then reset it, remap the direction through $08D4 and choose the corresponding facing animation.
Clear actor Y's active byte, Y low byte and sprite number (Y high is retained).
Select sound $0B, stop actor X's movement and begin animation stream index $38 with one-call delay and reload values.
Scan active slots 2 through 7 with a nonzero trigger width. Compute each trigger origin from its coordinate offsets, test Monty's overlap with $44EC and activate the trigger when carry is set.
Clear actor X's trigger width and hold state, set its animation delay/reload to 4 and select sound $0A for actor type 9.

Compare Monty's signed X/Y distances from a prepared trigger origin. Patch the width/height limits according to which side he approaches from. Return carry set for an accepted box overlap, clear for separation.
If actor X has either vertical direction bit set, toggle both bits $03.
If actor X has a horizontal direction bit set, toggle both bits $0C and select its facing animation.

When flag $20 is set and a random byte is below 8, clear the direction mask and choose vertical, horizontal or diagonal random movement according to the low two bits of the actor's turn mode, then update its animation.
When the random test is below 3, replace actor X's active countdown with a random value masked to seven bits.
Clear the actor's right, left, down or up direction bit when the corresponding terrain probe is class 3 or above.

Test active player attack slot 1 against slots 2 through 7, ignoring flashed, hidden and $FE-health actors. Apply weapon/strength damage from $805C, dispatch guardian damage separately and start actor destruction when its signed remaining health is zero or negative.

A flag can replace the struck actor with template $37. Otherwise mark it invulnerable, stop its movement, select the destruction animation and sound, then dispatch its nonzero score class through the code-address table at $83E7.
Damage selected from the weapon/strength table at $805C, consumed by ordinary actor and guardian hit handlers.

Convert actor X's attack coordinate to a cell using the weapon's collision offsets and fine scroll. Clamp the column, read the active screen row and translate its character through $AF00 into $87C8+X.

Outside shop state, probe the active attack's terrain and screen limits. A basic attack starts its impact animation; other weapons clear slot 1 and start a cooldown. Weapon type 1 converts the contact into an enlarged explosion through $4896.

For weapon type 1, retain slot 1, select the explosion sound and shape, offset the origin and configure its collision dimensions from strength. Strength 2 or 3 enables sprite expansion and moves the explosion origin farther up and left.
Five bytes, one for each level, all $80. Level start reads the entry for the level at $183D and stores it as both the attack delay $4936 and its reload $4937. Nothing writes the table.
Global enemy-attack countdown. The dispatcher waits for zero before searching for attackers.
Global enemy-attack countdown reload after a scan or a failure to find a free slot.
Source actor slot saved across projectile-template construction.
Low-byte X offset added to the source position when a projectile is placed.
Low-byte Y offset added to the source position when a projectile is placed.

Count down the global attack delay, then inspect active visible actors with attack flag 4 and no hold state. Find a free slot and dispatch the source actor's type to a projectile constructor. Reload the global delay after the scan or when no slot is free.
Create template $32 in the free slot, place it ten pixels above its source and select the attack sound.

Create template 0 at the source actor's centre, aim it towards Monty at speed 1 and select the attack sound. While a guardian is active ($835E nonzero) the level then decides: level 0 sets the health of slots 5-7 to $FF; level 1 gives the new actor animation index $1E with delay 2, multicolour, colour 8 and, when its X step is not zero, an X step of +1 or -1 from slot 5's direction; level 3 gives it shape $63, multicolour, colour 7 and 10-by-10 collision dimensions; levels 2 and 4 give it shape $6E and aim it again at speed 2.
On a random one-bit test, hold the source actor for $20 calls, clear its direction, select its charge animation and remember its slot for the background-flash routine.
On a random one-bit test, create template $38 at an 8-by-8 offset from the source, copy its direction and select the attack sound.
Create template $39 four pixels below an unheld source. Randomise its speed and direction mask, flash the source colour and select the attack sound.
Create template $3A at a 24-by-8 offset, hold the source's animation and select the attack sound. Source type $40 moves the new actor 48 pixels left and chooses its alternate source shape.
Create template $5E at a 24-by-1 offset and select the attack sound. Source type $80 changes the new animation stream and moves it 48 pixels left.

On a random one-bit test, create template $B8 with a two-pixel Y offset and copy the source direction. Choose source and projectile shapes from direction tables for types $A7 and $AE; the latter also changes dimensions and speed.
On a random one-bit test create template 0 at an 8-by-8 offset, select a direction-dependent source shape, configure motion mode 3 with removal on solid terrain and hold the source's animation.
On a random one-bit test, create template 0 eight pixels right of the source with motion mode 3, speed 4, solid-terrain removal, sprite $3B, colour 0 and 9-by-9 collision dimensions.

Create template 0 above the source, aim it at Monty at speed 3 and configure sprite $82, colour 8, type $EC, invulnerability and 18-by-18 dimensions. Set the new actor's active countdown to 30, which holds it for 29 calls.
Create template 0 at the source's centre, set downward motion mode 3, a three-pixel Y displacement and removal on solid terrain, then select the attack sound.
Create template $EC at the source's centre, choose random speed and horizontal direction bits, change the source colour and select the attack sound.
On a random bit-1 test, create template $F0 at the source centre with random speed 1 through 4 and a randomly mirrored horizontal direction.
On a random one-bit test, create template $DB at Y=$44 and X=$64 or $E4, with flags $60. Unlike the other constructors it requests no sound.

While the saved charge timer is active, shape $72 changes the level's shared colours and damages Monty when he is facing the tested side of the source and is outside climbing state. On expiry restore the colours and release the source's hold state.
Read a template pointer from $817C+Y into $B0/$B1, then populate actor X through $4F04.
Read 26 bytes through $B0/$B1 into actor X's display, health, flags, type, animation and motion arrays, duplicate its animation delay into the reload field and mark it active.
Use the saved source slot $4938 and half its collision dimensions as spawn offsets, then apply those offsets to the new actor X.
Copy source Y's coordinate high bytes into actor X, add X offset $4939 with carry, and add Y offset $493A to the low Y byte.
With a nonzero weapon type, count $7F7B to 50, decrement the remaining lifetime $7F7A when nonzero and reset the subcounter.

Compare six eight-byte names against the high-score name selected by $08E7. The stored candidates are offset by $45. The letter count is kept in $7126, the first pitch step of instrument stream 10, and stays there: 8 after a match, or the leading letters shared with JUGGLERS, which the music then adds to that instrument's notes. A match sets $08BE and resets base energy capacity, strength and reserve defaults, with per-name exceptions.
Six eight-byte high-score names stored with a $45 subtraction after initialisation, followed by the checker index byte. The checker adds $45 when comparing each byte.
Subtract $45 in place from 49 bytes beginning at $5076. The name checker adds $45 back when comparing a candidate with the entered high-score name.

When a screen rebuild is pending, remove other actors, disable the display, derive the map pointer from scroll position, fetch visible block columns and draw both screen buffers. Enable the display, initialise visible spawn records and adjust the scroll/spawn cursor for normal play.
Sixteen-bit camera position in character columns.
Sixteen-bit right limit for the selected level or current area.
Sixteen-bit pointer into the six-block-high map stream.
Character-column phase, 0 through 3, within a four-character-wide map block.
Gates incremental entering-column work after a full screen rebuild.
Sixteen character codes copied from one 4-by-4 map block before drawing or column expansion.
Descending index used to draw the block scratch through the screen-offset table.
One byte, 0, after the block draw index. No instruction names it and the indexed accesses to the block scratch at $5175 stop at index 15: nothing reads or writes it.
Three-bit horizontal fine scroll; a scroll step decrements it and wraps underflow to 7.
One-step scroll request consumed by $58BA.
Descending bytes 7 through 0 retained beside the scroll state.
One byte, 0, immediately before the block drawing routine. No instruction names it and the indexed accesses to the block scratch at $5175 stop at index 15: nothing reads or writes it.

Multiply block number A by 16 and address its 16 character codes at $B000. Copy them into $5175, then draw entries from index X down to zero using the 4-by-4 screen-offset table $51D4. Translate each character through $AE00 for its colour.
Sixteen screen offsets for a 4-by-4 block: four entries per row spaced 40 bytes vertically.
Block-buffer index constants retained beside the block screen offsets.
Descending block-placement index used when drawing both screens.
Visit 60 block positions described by the screen-address and block-index tables, drawing each 4-by-4 block into the $E800 and $EC00 screen buffers and their common colour RAM.

Patch seven source addresses from $5171/$5172, then copy eleven groups of seven bytes, read six bytes apart so that each group's seventh byte is the next group's first, into seven separate 11-byte arrays at $8D63-$8DAF, one for each byte of a group, indexed by group. Then advance the source pointer by 54 bytes.
Requests a one-character coarse shift into the inactive screen.
Requests the colour RAM update after a fine-scroll wrap.

When the coarse-scroll flag is set, copy playfield columns 1 through 39 from the active screen to columns 0 through 38 of the inactive screen, for 24 rows. Clear the flag and advance the world/column counters through $56C6.

When a colour update is pending, shift 24 colour rows one cell left (columns 1-39 to 0-38), then set column 39 of each row from the active screen's character there through $AE00. Clear the request and increment the completed-colour-update marker.
Multiply block number A by 16 to address its definition at $B000 and copy all 16 character codes into the block scratch buffer at $5175.
One byte, 0, between fetch_block_characters and the scroll-column increment routine. No instruction names it: nothing reads or writes it.
Increment the 16-bit scroll column. Every four columns reset the within-block index and advance the map-data source pointer by six bytes.

When playfield drawing is enabled, perform a pending coarse screen shift, fetch the next map blocks, expand them into four vertical character columns and draw the selected column at the screen's right edge.
Fetch seven block numbers from $8DB0, expand each 16-character block and distribute its four columns into four 28-byte vertical column buffers at $8C5D, $8C79, $8C95 and $8CB1.
Offsets selecting one of the four expanded 28-character columns for the current within-block phase.
Select a vertical character column using the within-block index and the offset table $574A. Write its first 24 rows into column 39 of the inactive screen buffer.
Patch the map source address from $5171/$5172, adding six bytes except when the within-block index is zero, then read seven block numbers into $8DB0.
Prevents requesting a second camera step before the pending one is consumed.

When a scroll step is requested, move active actors one pixel left and decrement the fine-scroll value. At underflow reset it to 7, switch the active screen and request its coarse screen and colour updates. Clear the one-step request latches.
Set the pending scroll-step and once-per-pass latch when a step has not already been requested.

Move each active actor one pixel left with borrow into its high X byte, applying the edge correction tested by the routine. Adjust the stored line-motion target on the corresponding half-resolution parity.
Unless inhibited, request a scroll step when Monty reaches X=222 or the next high-byte page and the scroll position is before the level's right limit. Add one point for an accepted request.

When activated, save selected actor coordinates and shapes, remove untyped actors, mark eligible targets and inhibit normal gameplay. Dispatch the current level's super-weapon style through $89AF, then restore saved state and consume its charge at the end.
Restore coordinates, sprite numbers and colours for the actor slots marked by $89CE.
For marked active slots 2 through 7, start the destruction animation and mark their health $FE.
Release the gameplay inhibition and super-weapon state, decrement its charge at $89CC and reactivate Monty.

Count to state $43, then restore and destroy the marked targets and finish. At state 3 convert marked shapes to copies of Monty; on intervening calls move them along per-slot direction and speed tables.

Count to state $43. Use Monty as a moving attack aimed successively at marked targets, selecting a destruction sprite as each target is reached. When targets are exhausted, aim him back at his saved location; finish after returning.

Move Monty's super-weapon line path, choose sprite $10 or $11 by horizontal direction and update trailing afterimages. The return-path state switches the super-weapon counter to $42 when its motion completes.
Shift seven entries of Monty's X-low, X-high and Y history, insert his current position and copy successive history entries into marked unused actor slots, with his shape and colour.
Stored prompt asking the player to enter a high-score name.

Requires fire to be released before a subsequent press can accept the entered name. The prompt copy at $5D7C draws 23 bytes from $5C15, one more than the 22-character prompt, so this byte also reaches the screen at $ECE7 as the character after the prompt.
Zero requests score ranking, one selects name entry, and $FF means the check or entry is finished.
Rank selected by the last-score comparison for inserting its name and digits.
Eight ranked six-digit scores followed by the last score, stored as numeric digits rather than character codes.
Eight eight-character names followed by the last-score label. Accepted names can also select secret game modifiers.
Eight saved screen character cells covered while the name is being edited.
Eight saved colour cells covered while the name is being edited.
Countdown between successive joystick edits in the name-entry routine.
Set after initialising the editable name field; cleared when fire accepts the name.
Name character position from 0 through 7.
Twenty-nine selectable characters: full stop, A through Z, space and question mark, followed by the alphabet terminator.
Index of the selected name character while processing joystick edits.
When the score-check state is zero call $FF70 to rank the score. When it is exactly 1, clear the background and update the name-entry routine.

Initialise an eight-character name field, saving its covered screen cells and colours. Use joystick up/down to cycle the 29-character alphabet and left/right to choose a position, with a repeat delay. A released-then-pressed fire accepts the name, shifts lower entries and stores the new name and six score digits.
Starting at the lower end, shift six-digit score records and eight-character names down one place until the insertion rank is reached.

Convert the saved score characters to numeric digits, convert nine score records to 24-bit values and compare the last score with eight ranked entries. Store its qualifying rank and set the name-entry state, or set that state to $FF when it does not qualify.
Three-byte conversion accumulator, low byte first ($5F56-$5F58), followed by six decimal digits copied from one score record ($5F59-$5F5E). Nothing reads or writes the last two bytes, $5F5F-$5F60.
Four-byte-spaced comparison slots for the ranked scores and last score; each meaningful value is 24-bit, most-significant byte first.
Low, middle and high bytes of the powers of ten used to convert six decimal digits into a 24-bit score.

X selects a six-digit record. Multiply each decimal digit by its split power-of-ten table through repeated addition, accumulate a 24-bit value and write it to the corresponding four-byte comparison slot.
Draw eight ranked six-digit scores and their eight-character names, plus the last score and its label, with fixed row colours.

Twenty little-endian pointers 64 bytes apart. The first sixteen address the 64-byte sound-effect records at $9C00-$9FC0. The last four hold $A000, $A040, $A080 and $A0C0, which are in the level's spawn records; every request in the code is for an effect from 0 to 15, so they are not used.
Nonzero prevents accepting a new sound-effect request.
Identifier of the accepted sound effect, also tested by gameplay to avoid restarting selected sounds.
One byte, 0, between the active effect identifier and the request flag. No instruction names it: nothing reads or writes it.
Nonzero requests the sound-effect record whose identifier is in $6106.
Sound-effect identifier used to index the pointer directory at $60DA.
Clear SID registers $D400-$D415 and set volume $D418 to 15.

When effects are enabled, a request is pending and no effect is active, consume the request, save its identifier and copy the first 26 bytes of its 64-byte record into the effect work area. Set a pending-initialisation flag.

Copy the rest of the effect record, initialise its two voice envelopes, pulse, pitch, waveform and filter state, reset SID registers and set the effect-active flag. Per-voice state occupies two work records separated by $30 bytes.

Complete pending effect initialisation, then run active voice lifetimes and effect envelopes. Update filter sweep, pulse width, waveform/gate and the two voices' pitch through the split frequency tables. Stop the effect when both lifetimes reach zero.

X=0 or $30 selects one effect voice. Advance its optional note sequence, delayed pitch sweep, pulse-width sequence, gate countdown and waveform sequence. The flags control which sequences repeat; updated state is written into the effect work record.
Marks an active sound effect and prevents another request from replacing it until the voice lifetimes finish.
Two effect-voice work records, separated by $30 bytes, with pitch, pulse, waveform, gate, sequence and duration state, plus shared filter work.

Last twelve bytes copied from the selected effect record. $65E4 packs the filter mode (high nibble, to $D418) and resonance (low nibble, to $D417); $65E5-$65E6 are the base cutoff, $65E7 the delay before the sweep, $65E8-$65E9 the sweep step and $65EA the reversal period; bit 7 of $65EB enables the filter. $65EC and $65ED are the sequence flags of voices 1 and 2, copied to $6584 and $65B4 at $6176. Nothing reads $65EE-$65EF.
Set after the first part of an effect record is copied; the next player call completes initialisation.
Waveform-control masks combined with each effect voice's gate bit.
High bytes of the sound-effects pitch lookup, indexed by base note plus current sequence offset.
Low bytes of the sound-effects pitch lookup, paired with the high-byte table at $65FA.
Second-last low byte of the effects pitch lookup (index 94 of $665A); the final byte follows at $66B9.
Final byte of the effects pitch lookup; the countdown routine begins at $66BA.
Increment the border colour, then decrement the third-voice countdown when nonnegative. After it becomes negative, clear SID voice-3 registers $D40E-$D413.

Increment the shared background colour, and when the countdown is negative and its extra gate is zero, initialise SID voice 3 with frequency $1388, control $81, zero envelopes and a four-step countdown.
Countdown used by the separate third-voice sound entry at $66BA.
Additional gate tested by the separate third-voice sound entry at $66D3.
Requested tune number compared with $6700 at the start of the music player.
Tune number whose order-list pointers the music player has installed.

Reinitialise when the requested tune changes. When enabled, write the filter and volume, count the song tick and process three voices. Read pattern commands and notes on the voice's tick boundary, otherwise advance instrument waveform, pulse, filter, pitch sequence, vibrato and glide state before writing SID registers.

Restore a voice's pattern pointer and byte index, then interpret its next note or command. $FF advances the order list or restores a saved pattern, high nibbles select tempo, volume/glide, instrument and note duration, and $61-$65 control loops, calls, jumps and transposition.
Mark the voice as gliding, read its packed glide timing and target-note offset, apply the voice transpose and continue pattern parsing.

Select a five-bit instrument number and, when it changes, load waveform/gate, envelope, pulse and filter settings from the split instrument tables. Return to the pattern stream after the instrument command.

Distinguish the note byte from control commands $61-$65. The commands maintain a per-voice pattern return/loop stack, change the pattern pointer or set transposition. An ordinary nonzero note looks up its pitch and resets instrument-envelope state.

Select an instrument's timed waveform sequence or pitch/control stream. Its command bytes can hold or loop the stream; ordinary entries update pitch, waveform and the stream index before pulse and filter work.
Count an instrument's pulse delay, then alternate the configured upward and downward pulse-width ramps. Reload repeating ramp counts from the instrument tables when required.
For an instrument with filter flag 8, select a timed filter adjustment from $7050/$7055 and write its cutoff. Continue through glide or vibrato processing.

Derive a fractional semitone step from adjacent frequency-table entries and an instrument shift count. Advance a triangular phase and add the appropriate signed pitch displacement after the configured delay.

When glide is active, derive the difference between the current and target pitches, divide it by the packed timing and tempo span, and apply its signed step. On reaching the target, copy the target note's frequency and clear the glide flag.
Write voice X's frequency, pulse width and waveform/control to SID registers using its saved register offset, then move to the preceding voice or return.
Read the voice's next pattern pointer from its order list. A zero pointer restarts the order index at zero. Store the resulting low/high pattern pointer in the voice work arrays.

Save tune A and reset music state. A negative tune selects the stop path. Otherwise read three order-list pointers from the tune directory, initialise instrument and pattern indices, fetch each first pattern and enable music playback.

Reset the music work area and SID registers, then store X=$FF left by the reset loop into the requested tune, loaded tune and playback-state bytes. The negative playback state stops the frame player until another tune is requested.
Clear 200 bytes of music work memory starting after $6D42, then write 8 followed by zero to SID registers $D400-$D418.
SID register offsets 0, 7 and 14 for the three music voices.
Masks used to remove one voice's filter-routing bit before applying an instrument setting.
Filter-routing bit values for the three SID voices.
Per-voice starting offsets into the music pattern loop/call stack.
Pattern call and loop stack storage, cleared on music initialisation. Each voice uses its own starting offset.
Playback-state byte tested by sign before the music tick is processed.
Combined SID mode and volume byte written to $D418.
SID resonance and filter-routing byte written to $D417.
Tick reload selected by a pattern tempo command.
Countdown pacing the pattern note-duration counters.
Saved voice-array index while instrument work temporarily uses X for other tables.
Saved SID register offset for the music voice being processed.
Three-entry arrays for pattern stack/index, order pointer, pattern pointer, instrument, duration, pitch, waveform, pulse, modulation and glide state. The player at $6701 indexes them by voice.
Low bytes of the music player's note-frequency lookup; its paired high bytes begin at $6E6A.
High bytes of the music note-frequency lookup, paired with $6E0A.

Three six-byte descriptors at $6ECA, $6ED0 and $6ED6, chosen by an instrument's $6F9B value of $80, $86 or $8C, followed from $6EDC to $6F2E by the sequences they point to. A descriptor holds the address of a timed waveform sequence, whose first byte is the number of calls it lasts, the address of a frequency-high sequence, a frequency-low byte and a value added to the frequency high; $696D patches them into its operands at $69A9-$69BF.
Parallel instrument tables for control, envelope, pulse, waveform sequence, vibrato and modulation settings; the instrument parser and per-frame voice updater index them by instrument number.
Three low bytes of the order-list pointers for tune 0; the corresponding high bytes are at $7052.
Three high bytes of the tune-0 order-list pointers, paired with $704F.
Timed filter-step constants used by the instrument filter envelope.
Low bytes of the pitch/control-stream pointers used by $69C6, paired with $7069.

High bytes of the pitch/control-stream pointers used by $69C6, for indexes 0-11. The first byte, $2D, is also the low byte of index 11, because the low table at $705E holds only eleven entries: index 11 points to $712D.
Variable-length instrument pitch/control streams. Values $80 and $81 hold or loop; ordinary entries are paired pitch offsets and waveform-control values.

Instrument pitch/control streams 10 ($7126-$712C, $705E/$7069 index 10) and 11 ($712D-$7136, index 11), then the three tune-0 order lists at $7137, $7187 and $71D7, each 39 pattern pointers and a zero pointer, then from $7227 the pattern streams, which run without a gap to $7B30. $7126 itself is also the name checker's letter counter ($5001), which changes stream 10's first pitch offset.
Bytes from $7526 continue music_pattern_data ($7126), described at $7126.

Bytes from $7926 continue the pattern streams of music_pattern_data ($7126) as far as $7B30, where the last pattern ends. $7B31-$7B37 is the text THE END, and nothing reads it or the bytes after it to $7D25: no order list, pattern or instruction reaches them.
Bytes from $7D26 to $7EBF, after the music data ($7126), which ends at $7B30 with the text THE END after it. No order list, pattern or instruction reaches them: nothing reads or writes them.
Resident per-level background/shared colour tables, mutable trail character choices and related rendering values used by the raster handlers and terrain-trail drawing.
Slot of the actor currently supporting Monty, or zero.
Death stage counter advanced by $1A9A.
Subcounter spacing changes of the death stage.

Inhibition state written by death ($1A90) and the temporary hazard response ($23D0-$2412). Its one reader is the play handler at $0A26, which skips Monty's animation and the updates after it while it is nonzero.
Countdown controlling a temporary hazard response and alternate Monty animation selection.
Index into the Monty shape stream at $7EF9.
Countdown before advancing Monty's shape stream.

Sprite-number sequences selected by movement and facing, from $7EF9 to $7F34; $80 followed by an index loops a sequence. The last six bytes are two tables of attack-pose sprites indexed by facing/4 (1 left, 2 right): $7F35 for the basic attack, read at $327D, and $7F38 for the shatterbomb throw, read at $3292.
Eight per-actor hit-flash countdowns. Monty's ordinary damage routine refuses another hit while his counter is nonzero.
Movement states 0 standing, 1 walking, 2 jumping, 3 falling and 4 climbing.
Saved movement state used to choose a new Monty animation sequence.
Signed vertical displacements for Monty's jump. $80 is the trajectory's terminator.
Index of the next displacement in the jump trajectory.
Saved horizontal direction mask used for walking animation, shots and sliding.
Previous facing value used to detect changes of animation.
Horizontal intent captured when a jump starts and applied during its trajectory.
Counter used to space the class-9 terrain jump/damage response.
Remaining energy units; the status bar draws one full segment per pair.
Unsigned one-byte shop currency, displayed as up to three decimal digits.
Strength index 0 through 3, selecting attack shapes, dimensions and damage tables.
Remaining timed-weapon lifetime units, decremented after each 50 updates of $7F7B.
Counts to 50 before decrementing the timed weapon's lifetime.
Selected attack type, 0 through 3; zero selects Monty's basic attack.

Countdown for Monty's attack pose, set to 6 when a basic attack starts ($3288) or a shatterbomb is thrown ($329D). When a basic attack's count reaches zero the attack slot is cleared and its cooldown begins ($34A5). Nothing reads or writes the second byte, $7F7E.
Saved direction of the active player attack, also used by the homing turner.
Horizontal collision-probe adjustment selected from weapon and strength tables.
Vertical collision-probe adjustment selected from weapon and strength tables.

Number of one-pixel recoil steps still to apply to Monty after he fires weapon type 2 or 3: $32A8 sets it to 4 and takes one step at once, and $32C6 takes one more on each call while it is nonzero. The steps go through the terrain-aware movement routines and move him away from the way he faces.
Monty's facing divided by four, saved at $32B2 when weapon type 2 or 3 is fired. It steers the recoil steps counted in $7F82: 2 (facing right) moves him left, and 1 (facing left) moves him right.

$7F84 holds the attack's shape from the table at $7F88, saved at $32F6 when any attack starts. A basic attack starts with shape 0, and this shape is put back, with the impact animation, when it hits an actor ($46C3) or is stopped by the terrain or the screen's limits ($4871). The three bytes after it, 42 43 44, are not used: no instruction names or reaches them.
Shape lookup indexed by strength times four plus weapon type.
Four weapon-specific colour bytes for attack sprite slot 1.
Countdown preventing the next player attack while nonzero.
Index into the signed weapon-1 vertical trajectory.
Nonzero changes the weapon-1 projectile into its stationary explosion state.
Signed vertical offsets used by the moving weapon-1 projectile; its $80 marker repeats the last indexed displacement.
Weapon/strength dependent selectors and X/Y offsets used to place the player attack relative to Monty and his facing.
Bytes from $8000 continue weapon_spawn_offsets ($7FCA), described at $7FCA.

Eighteen four-byte tables indexed by strength. Terrain-probe X and Y offsets for weapon type 0 ($8011, $8015), type 2 ($8021, $8025) and type 3 ($8029, $802D); $8019-$8020 are zero and not read, type 1 taking zero offsets from the code. Collision width and height for type 0 ($8031, $8035), type 1 ($8039, $803D), type 2 ($8041, $8045) and type 3 ($8049, $804D), and for the shatterbomb explosion ($8051, $8055, read at $48E7).
Countdown spacing one-step changes of the homing weapon's eight-way direction.
Delay before the strongest type-2 weapon begins following an eligible target.
Actor slot searched by the strongest type-2 weapon.
Damage values indexed by weapon type times four plus strength.
Number of exit records searched for each of the five levels.
Zero for a top-screen exit, one for a bottom-screen exit.
Per-exit background choices read when moving between final-level areas.
Shop state: 0 outside a shop, 1 on entry, 2 after the companion sprite is set up, and the price plus 2 when an item is bought, counted down by $1446 as it is paid for.
Item-type indexed shop prices.
Price of the currently contacted shop item; zero when no priced item is selected.
Actor slot of the shop item selected for purchase.
The last horizontal joystick push ($DC00 AND $0C) seen while paying; a different push keeps that call's coin.
Five 12-byte records. Each holds two six-byte scroll/position destinations for entering and leaving the shop.
Delay suppressing immediate shop re-entry; its expiry also removes active item type 9.
Countdown for a temporary shop response message.
Identifier of the temporary price/purchase response shown by the shop-message routine.
Sixteen-character shop item and response strings, selected by item type or response number.
First eleven little-endian pointers of the actor-template directory; the level-loaded continuation begins at $8192.

The last six bytes of the four-byte random-spawn records that begin in the level load at $837E. No instruction names them; $3D2B reaches them through a pointer only in level 4, the Bermuda Triangle, whose mask $0F ($8373) and base $83A6 select sixteen records, $83A6-$83E5. Record 14 is D2 04 at $83DE in the level load followed by 10 DB here; record 15 is F5 04 0C D2 at $83E2-$83E5. Bytes 0 and 1 are the position (low, high), 2 the row and 3 the template. $83E6, which follows, is the current level number.
Level identifier accepted after the loader compares the requested number with its payload.
Eight little-endian code addresses for actor score classes, from one point through the 20000-point entry.
Stored final-score label displayed during the quit transition.
The final-scene label followed by the five fixed-width level names used by the selector and final-score display.
Five offsets into the level-title string block.
Delay before the completed-game message accepts a fire press.
Six 36-character lines congratulating Monty on retrieving the scrolls.
Six rows of 21 character codes drawing the title logo in the title character set.

Mutable terrain-class probes around Monty, filled by $2881: his left side at $85F4-$85F7 and $8602, his right side at $85F8-$85FB and $8603, the centre column at $85FE (upper) and $85FF (lower), and the two head probes at $8600 and $8601. $85FC and $85FD are not used: no instruction names or reaches them.
Six arrays of eight terrain-class samples, filled by $3E9F for active actor slots.

Character codes for the level selector's five framed level pictures, 22 rows of six, copied to the screen by $261B. $8634 is the top frame row and $8652 the bottom one, each drawn five times. The other twenty rows are four for each picture, starting at $863A, $8658, $8670, $8688 and $86A0: a frame character ($60, $61) either side of four picture characters, which run from $65 to $B4 in the title character set, sixteen to a picture.
Eight active-low column masks driven through CIA1 port A by the full keyboard scanner.
Eight row-bit masks used to find the first pressed key within a column.

Translation from the scanned key position to a command or character byte: 64 bytes indexed by column number times eight plus row number ($0EE0). The last two bytes of the item, $8A6E and $8A6F, are work bytes in which $0ECF and $0ED2 keep the column and row numbers.
Inverted row bits saved while scanning the keyboard.
Translated pressed key, or zero when the scan finds none.
Column masks indexed by the command byte in the single-key test routine.
Row-bit masks paired with the single-key column table.
Countdown selecting the next level-specific character-memory animation update.

Two-call divider for the rotating glyph rows at $F398-$F3A7: $1175 counts it down and reloads it with 2, in levels 0, 1 and 4 only (levels 2 and 3 return first and leave it as it is). The conveyor terrain classes 5 and 6 read it too: $2FE3 and $2FFE move Monty one pixel left or right on the calls where it is 1.
Saved fire test while the level-selector raster handler resolves the current marker.

Last selector direction: the joystick's left/right bits as read ($DC00 AND $0C, so 4 is right and 8 is left), or Monty's facing with those bits inverted when he reaches the marker of a completed level. While Monty is away from the requested level's marker, $0D89 walks him one pixel right when it is 4 and left otherwise.
Five low X coordinates compared with Monty when choosing a level marker.
Five high X coordinates paired with $8B8C.
Sprite position-register offsets 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12 and 14.
Three bytes, 10 12 14, which carry on the sequence of sprite register offsets at $8B96 past sprite 7. Nothing uses them: no instruction names them, and $0F23 reads the table with X from 0 to 7 only.
Stored fire-to-play prompt and copyright strings copied into the title screen.
Number of full energy segments computed by the status renderer.
Colour choices for the 40-column status row, with the extra byte read by its inclusive initialiser.

Guardian tables and counters. $8C0C-$8C13: four pairs of shapes for slots 4 to 7, the first of a pair when bit 3 of slot 5's direction $8795 is clear and the second when it is set ($1ED4). $8C14: a counter, the Amazon guardian's 65-call phase counter ($1FAD) and the Bermuda guardian's index into its commands ($21E9). $8C15-$8C16: the two X positions $2011 picks between at random for the Amazon guardian. $8C17-$8C1A and $8C1B-$8C1E: animation indexes for slots 6 and 7, one of four picked at random at $1FDD, a zero leaving the index as it is. $8C1F: the Bermuda guardian's countdown to its next command, reloaded with 32 ($21DC). $8C20-$8C3E: its commands 0 to 3, read from $8C21 on, one each time the countdown ends, with $FF sending the index back to zero.
Prepared trigger X-low, X-high and Y values, followed by overlap distance scratch and supporting-actor displacement.
World column being considered for actor spawning, record offset and visible-column progress.
Direction-mask to circular-index mapping and its inverse, used for one-step homing turns.
Four expanded 28-character vertical columns, scratch output of the block-column decoder.

$8CCD is the destination index and $8CCE the source block index while $5705 expands seven map blocks into the vertical character columns. $8CCF, $28, is the low byte of the first screen-row pointer of the table that carries on at $8CD0.

Screen-row pointers, low byte first, starting one byte earlier at $8CCF: 37 for the $E800 buffer ($8CCF-$8D18), then 37 for the $EC00 buffer ($8D19-$8D62). In each table the first eight point to screen row 1 ($E828, $EC28), the next 22 to rows 2 to 23 and the last seven to row 24 ($EBC0, $EFC0), so a row above or below the play area reads the nearest row inside it. The terrain probes ($27E7, $2881, $3E9F, $4780) and $3DD6 index them with twice a row number, from several base addresses.
Mutable map blocks fetched for rebuilding the screens.
Seven block numbers for the next entering map column, written by $5882 and read by $5705. The eighth byte, $8DB7, is not used.

Low bytes of 70 block-drawing destination addresses in the $EC00 buffer, ten to a row, four characters apart, with rows 160 bytes apart from $EC28. $51EC uses the first 60, six rows of blocks; the last ten, $EFE8-$F00C, would be a seventh row past the end of the screen and are not read.
High bytes paired with the block-drawing addresses at $8DB8.

Indexes into the visible-block buffer at $8D63 for the 60 on-screen block positions, six rows of ten that skip the eleventh block of each buffer row. The last four bytes of the item, 42 43 44 45, begin a seventh row that $51EC never reads.

Sixty bytes that nothing reads. $8E84-$8E89 are six more block-buffer indexes, $46-$4B, finishing a seventh row of ten that begins at $8E80; $51EC uses only indexes 0-59 of the table at $8E44. $8E8A-$8E92 are the text END AGAIN, $8E93 is $EA, and $8E94-$8EBF are zero.
Shared first 64 bytes of the actor shape stream. The level-loaded continuation begins at $8F00; $FF followed by a byte loops or removes an actor.

The end of the Klondike Mine's path streams, which begin in its level load at $96D8 and run on into this resident page. $9B00-$9B34: the rest of magnitude stream 15, which starts at $9AEC, to its $FC. $9B35-$9B7D: magnitude stream 16. $9B7E-$9BC5: the direction stream that streams 15 and 16 share. $9BC6-$9BDA: magnitude stream 17, ending $FF. $9BDB-$9BEE: its direction stream. $9BEF-$9BFF: zero. $418E reads them through Klondike's pointers at $90E0 and $9104; no other level's pointers or streams reach this page.
Sixteen 64-byte effect-record slots addressed by $60DA, holding two voice envelopes and shared filter parameters.
Shared sprite shape bytes in VIC bank $C000. Each 64-byte slot holds 21 rows of three bytes followed by one unused byte.
Bytes from $C400 continue resident_sprite_shapes ($C000), described at $C000.
Bytes from $C800 continue resident_sprite_shapes ($C000), described at $C000.
Bytes from $CC00 continue resident_sprite_shapes ($C000), described at $C000.

Resident sprite shapes $38-$3F in 64-byte slots, carrying on after the level-loaded shapes $35-$37 at $CD40-$CDFF. The resident shapes run on at $D000-$D3FF, in the RAM beneath I/O, as shapes $40-$4F; each level load supplies shapes $50-$9F at $D400-$E7FF.
Continuation of the resident sprite slots from $CE00, beneath the CPU's I/O view. The VIC reads their 21-by-3-byte shapes from RAM.

First 224 glyph slots of the resident character allocation used by the title and status-band raster handlers. The upper 32 slots at $FF00 are overlaid by cleared loader-prompt space, the high-score helper and hardware vectors.
Bytes from $FC00 continue status_and_title_charset ($F800), described at $F800.

Text for the level loader's two-line message, all zero bytes on this disk. A 31-character first line at $FF00 for levels 0 and 1 and another at $FF1F for levels 2 to 4, chosen through the two pointers at $FF5D ($FF00, $FF1F), and a 31-character second line at $FF3E. $1630 still copies them to rows 10 and 12 of the $EC00 screen, nine NOPs follow at $164B, and the screen is then cleared. $FF61-$FF62 hold a third pointer, $FF3E, that nothing reads, and $FF63-$FF6F are zero.
Disable raster interrupts, clear the screen and rank the last score, then acknowledge and re-enable the raster interrupt before returning.

Zero bytes after the high-score helper, except $FFB8-$FFBF: FF, six bytes of 81 and FF, the eight rows of a hollow box, which is character $F7 of the character set at $F800. No instruction names these bytes, and none is run as code.
One zero byte in the run of zeros from $FFC0 to $FFF9, between the box glyph at $FFB8 and the vectors at $FFFA. No instruction names it.
Retained tail of the status character allocation, including cleared bytes before the hardware vectors at $FFFA. This span begins at $FFC8.
NMI, reset and IRQ vectors written by the game to $0E69, $0E6A and $0E79 respectively.
